---
applyTo: "spec/**/*.rb"
---

# RSpec and FactoryBot

- Check the details in unit specs, e.g. model, service and action specs: the values the code works out, the errors it raises, and what each error holds. In integration specs, e.g. request, feature and job specs, check only the outline: whether the code succeeded or failed, and what it did as a whole. Leave each detail to the unit spec for the code that works it out, e.g. check a report's context with `published_post.to_honeybadger_context` in a request spec, and the hash it returns in the model spec.
- Only sign in a user, e.g. with `sign_in`, in request and feature specs. In other specs, pass the user in as an argument, e.g. `Posts::PublishPost.call(post, publisher: user)`.
- When you add or change an action, cover in request and feature specs what each persona can do, and on which records. Include a persona who can act on some records but not this one, e.g. a user who did not create the record.
- In request and feature specs, you MUST NOT cover a persona whose role plays no part in the action. The User persona covers it, and so does the policy spec.
- List personas in rank order in request and feature specs, as in permission checks, e.g. `context "as an app admin"` before `context "as a publishing manager"`, then `context "as a user"` and `context "when not signed in"`.
- Put spec setup in `spec/support`, not in `spec/rails_helper.rb`, with one file for each gem or concern, named after it, each with its own `RSpec.configure` block, e.g. `config.include FactoryBot::Syntax::Methods` in `spec/support/factory_bot.rb`.
- When a spec checks a time, or the code works one out, call `travel_to` on the example's first line, with a blank line after it, and match each time exactly with `eq`, e.g. `expect(post.reload.archived_at).to eq(Time.zone.now)`. You MUST NOT match a time with `be_within` or `an_instance_of(ActiveSupport::TimeWithZone)`.
- Use `travel_to Time.zone.now` when the spec only needs the clock to stop. When the code depends on the date, pass a fixed time that tests it, e.g. `travel_to Time.zone.local(2026, 10, 31, 23, 59)` for code that works out the end of a month. You MUST NOT pass `with_usec: true` to `travel_to`.
- Avoid passing a block to `travel_to`, e.g. `travel_to(time) do ... end`. Call it on its own line.
- You MAY declare `let(:current_time) { Time.zone.now.change(usec: 0) }` as the first line of the top-level `describe` block, and build times from it, e.g. `current_time - 13.months`. Drop the microseconds, because `travel_to` stops the clock on a whole second. When the spec's fixtures only work at one time, set it to that time instead, e.g. `let(:current_time) { Time.zone.local(2026, 3, 14, 9, 30) }`.
- Stop the clock at `current_time` in a `before` on the line after the `let`, e.g. `before { travel_to current_time }`, not on an example's first line. Every example then runs with the clock stopped, and the `before` runs ahead of every `let!` and `before` below it, so their records get the stopped time too.
- With the clock stopped at `current_time`, move it with `travel` when the code depends on time passing, e.g. `travel 31.minutes` for a token that expires after 30 minutes. Set `created_at` on each record when the spec checks their order, because records an example creates get the same time.
- When some examples depend on the date, put them in a context named for the time, e.g. `context "on a leap day"`, and override `current_time` with a fixed time that tests it, e.g. `let(:current_time) { Time.zone.local(2028, 2, 29, 12) }`. The context doesn't need its own `travel_to`, because the top-level `before` reads the overridden time.
- Call `dom_id` on its own in specs, e.g. `dom_id(comment)`. You MUST NOT write `ActionView::RecordIdentifier.dom_id(comment)`.
- In request and feature specs, prefer a Capybara matcher for the element over `have_content` or `include`, e.g. `have_link`, `have_button`, `have_field`, `have_select`, or `have_css` with `text:`, e.g. `expect(page).to have_css("h1", text: "Hello World")` instead of `expect(page).to have_content("Hello World")` or `expect(response.body).to include("Hello World")`.
- When checking a select's options with `with_options:`, check one option on each line, e.g. `expect(response.body).to have_select("Status", with_options: ["Draft"])` and `expect(response.body).to have_select("Status", with_options: ["Published"])`. You MUST NOT list several options in one check, e.g. `with_options: ["Draft", "Published"]`.
- In request and feature specs, you MUST NOT compare the whole body, e.g. `expect(response.body).to eq(...)` or a snapshot. Check each value with its own matcher.
- For a role or flag on the whole app, build the user with a factory trait, e.g. `let(:user) { create(:user, :<role>) }`. Give the user factory one trait for each, named after it and defined in rank order. Use a plain `create(:user)` for the User persona, who has no role.
- You MUST NOT add a user trait for a role on one record. Build a plain `create(:user)` and give it the role on the record, e.g. as the record's owner or through a membership. For a persona with more than one role, build the user with the trait for the whole-app role, then give it the role on the record.
- In request specs, write persona contexts only for actions where access depends on the user. For an action that does not check a user, e.g. an API with a shared token or a callback from another service, leave out persona contexts and write one `context` for each way the request can be authenticated, e.g. `context "with an access token"`, `context "with an invalid access token"` and `context "without an access token"`.
- In request specs, write one `context` for each persona whose role plays a part in the action, and for the User and the Guest, in rank order. Name each persona context after its role on the whole app, or a role it holds through membership of a parent record, as `"as a <persona>"`, e.g. `context "as a publishing manager"` or `context "as a magazine editor"`, or `context "as a user"` for a persona with neither. Put the Guest last, as `context "when not signed in"`. Use `"as a"` only for persona contexts, e.g. `context "with a Turbo Stream"`, not `"as a Turbo Stream"`.
- In request specs, when the persona's role is on the record under test, describe the record in a second argument to `context`, with the role after it as `"as the <record role>"`, e.g. `context "as a user", "with a post as the author"`. For a persona that also has a role on the whole app, put that role in the first argument, e.g. `context "as a copy editor", "with a post as the author"`.
- In request specs, when a context uses a record the persona has no role on, describe that record in the second argument, e.g. `context "as a user", "with a post written by another user"`. When a context needs the record in a particular state, put the state in the record's description, e.g. `context "as a user", "with a draft post as the author"`.
- In request specs, set up each persona inside its context as a signed-in `user`. Define `user` and the records the persona needs in each context, not in the `describe` block above. You MUST NOT define a `let` per persona, e.g. `let(:<role>)`.
- In request specs, the user MAY have a person's name, e.g. Jane Tester, but still give its role in the context name.
- In request specs, give a membership persona its membership in the persona's `let`s with `let!`, so it exists before the request, e.g. `let!(:magazine) { create_magazine_with_magazine_editor(user) }` after `let(:user) { create(:user) }`.
- You SHOULD give each membership role a spec helper named `create_<parent>_with_<role>` that takes the user, gives it the role and returns the parent record, e.g. `def create_magazine_with_magazine_editor(user) = create(:magazine, editors: [user])`. Put it in the parent's `SpecHelpers` module, e.g. `MagazineSpecHelpers` in `spec/support/magazine_spec_helpers.rb`, included for every spec type that sets up the persona, e.g. `type: :request`. Use it instead of building the membership inline.
- In request specs, when a membership persona's examples act on different records, e.g. a post in its magazine and a post in another magazine, write one context with no second argument, e.g. `context "as a magazine editor"`. Build each record in the example that needs it, and name the example after where the record sits, e.g. `it "updates a post in the magazine"` with `create(:post, magazine:)`, and `it "does not update a post in another magazine"`. Use this shape whenever the spec covers a record outside the membership.
- In request specs, when every example for a membership persona acts on the same record, describe it in the second argument with its state and where it sits, e.g. `context "as a magazine editor", "with a draft post in the magazine"` with `let(:draft) { create(:post, magazine:, published_at: nil) }`. Cover records outside the membership in a context with no second argument next to it, e.g. `context "as a magazine editor"` with `it "does not update a post in another magazine"`.
- In request specs, a membership persona's role on the record under test still goes in the second argument, e.g. `context "as a magazine editor", "with a post as the author"`. Build that record in the persona's magazine, e.g. `create(:post, magazine:, author: user)`.
- In request specs, for a persona with a role on the whole app and a membership role, name both in the first argument, highest first, e.g. `context "as a publishing manager as a magazine editor"`.
- Rank membership personas with the app's other personas, by the app's persona list, e.g. a Magazine Editor after a Copy Editor.
- In request specs, check the status of every response that is not a redirect with `have_http_status`, e.g. `expect(response).to have_http_status(:ok)`. Leave a blank line above and below that line. Pass it a named status, e.g. `have_http_status(:not_found)` or `have_http_status(:unprocessable_content)`. You MUST NOT pass a number, e.g. `have_http_status(404)`.
- In request specs, you MUST NOT check a status with `be_successful`, `be_ok`, `be_redirect`, `be_not_found` or a status type, e.g. `have_http_status(:success)`. Some accept a range of statuses, e.g. `be_successful` passes for a `204` when `PostsController#show` has to return `200`, and none say which status came back when they fail.
- In request specs, check every redirect with `redirect_to`, e.g. `expect(response).to redirect_to(post_path(draft))`. On the next line, check the flash with the `have_flash_<key>` matcher for its key, which checks the whole flash, e.g. `expect(flash).to have_flash_notice("Post was updated.")`. You MUST NOT check a single flash key, e.g. `expect(flash[:notice]).to eq("Post was updated.")`, or compare the flash hash by hand, e.g. `expect(flash.to_hash).to match("notice" => "Post was updated.")`. You MUST NOT check a redirect with `have_http_status(:found)` or `be_redirect`.
- In request specs, check each header the controller sets itself, e.g. `expect(response.headers["Content-Disposition"]).to eq("attachment; filename=\"hello-world.pdf\"; filename*=UTF-8''hello-world.pdf")` for `send_data pdf, filename: "#{post.slug}.pdf"`, or `expect(response.headers["Location"]).to eq(api_v1_post_url(Post.last))` for `location: api_v1_post_url(@post)`. You MAY check other headers. You MUST NOT check the `Location` of a redirect, because the `redirect_to` matcher already checks it. Put the header checks below the status, or below the redirect and the flash, and above the checks on the body, with a blank line above and below them.
- In request specs, when an action responds with `head :no_content`, check the status and what the action changed, e.g. `expect(response).to have_http_status(:no_content)` after `expect { delete api_v1_post_path(published_post), headers: headers }.to change(Post, :count).by(-1)`. You SHOULD NOT check the body, e.g. `expect(response.body).to be_empty`, because Rails drops the body of every `204` response.
- When an action shows a form again because the input isn't valid, check the status, that nothing changed, and that the form shows the error the example's params cause, e.g. `expect(response.body).to have_field_error("Title can't be blank")`. Check errors with the helpers in `spec/support/form_spec_helpers.rb`: `have_field_error` for an error on a field, and `have_form_error` for an error on `:base`, e.g. `expect(response.body).to have_form_error("Post could not be rejected.")`. You SHOULD NOT write the error's selector in a spec, e.g. `have_css(".invalid-feedback", text: "Title can't be blank")`.
- In request specs, when a page shows several records, check each value about one of them inside that record's element, with a matcher named `have_<resource>` that takes the record and passes Capybara's options through, e.g. `expect(response.body).to have_comment(comment, text: "Great post!")` with `def have_comment(comment, **options) = have_css("##{dom_id(comment)}", **options)` in `CommentSpecHelpers`. Check that a record isn't shown with `not_to`, e.g. `expect(response.body).not_to have_comment(hidden_comment)`.
- In request specs, you SHOULD check a record with its `have_<resource>` matcher. When the check is about an element inside the record's, e.g. a button, you MAY find the record's element with a helper named `find_<resource>`, assign it to a local variable, and check it on the next line, e.g. `comment_element = find_comment(comment)` then `expect(comment_element).to have_button("Approve")`, with `def find_comment(comment) = Capybara.string(response.body).find("##{dom_id(comment)}")`. Put it in a module named after the resource with a `RequestSpecHelpers` suffix, e.g. `CommentRequestSpecHelpers`, included only for `type: :request`, in the same file as the resource's spec helpers module. You MUST NOT write the record's selector out, e.g. `have_css("#comment_#{comment.id}")`.
- In request specs, you SHOULD NOT follow a redirect with `follow_redirect!`. Check the redirect, and check the page it goes to in that page's own GET example, with the record set up in the state the action leaves it in. Follow the redirect only when the spec can't set up the next request's session beforehand, e.g. a Devise route that signs the user in.
- In request specs, when the action renders a page with `flash.now`, check the message in the response body with a matcher for the element that shows it, e.g. `expect(response.body).to have_css("[role='alert']", text: "This post is archived.")`. You MUST NOT check a `flash.now` message with a flash matcher, e.g. `expect(flash).to have_flash_alert("This post is archived.")`.
- In request specs, make one request per example and check everything about it in that example, e.g. the change, the redirect and the flash after `post posts_path`. You MUST NOT repeat the same request in several examples with one check each.
- In request specs, tag each action's `describe` block with `:aggregate_failures`, e.g. `describe "POST /posts", :aggregate_failures do`.
- In request specs, wrap a request that changes records in `expect { }.to change`, e.g. `expect { post posts_path, params: { post: { title: "Hello World" } } }.to change(Post, :count).by(1)` or `.to change { draft.reload.title }.to("New title")`. Use `not_to change` when the request changes nothing.
- In feature specs, use `RSpec.feature` named after the feature under test, e.g. `RSpec.feature "Post Publishing"`, and write each example as a `scenario`.
- In feature specs, start each scenario name with the persona carrying out the task, then what they want to achieve, e.g. `scenario "<Persona> publishes a post"`. Order scenarios by persona rank.
- In feature specs, write scenarios for what a persona can do. You MUST NOT write scenarios for actions a persona is not allowed to take. The only exceptions are a regression, e.g. a bug that let the persona do it before, or a critical action, e.g. keeping drafts hidden from Guests.
- In feature specs, carry out several actions in one scenario, e.g. find a post, open it, publish it, then check it is listed. You MUST NOT write one scenario per request.
- In feature specs, put a `# GIVEN`, `# WHEN` or `# THEN` comment above each step: `GIVEN` for setup, `WHEN` for what the persona does, `THEN` for what they see. Write the comments in the first person, as the persona describing the situation and what they do, e.g. `# GIVEN I am signed in as a <Persona>`. Start a step with `# AND` when it follows a step of the same type, e.g. `# WHEN I open the post` then `# AND I publish it`. Leave a blank line before each comment, except the first in the scenario. A scenario MAY repeat `WHEN` and `THEN`. Keep the `GIVEN` steps together at the start, except a `GIVEN` that sets up a mocked response, which MAY go just before the step that needs it, e.g. `# GIVEN the newsletter service accepts the post` before `# WHEN I publish it`.
- You MUST NOT use `let` or `let!` in feature specs. Build every record in the scenario, under its `# GIVEN` and `# AND` comments, e.g. `create(:post, title: "Hello World")` under `# AND there is a draft post`.
- In feature specs, when a page shows several records, scope each step about one of them with a helper named `within_<resource>` that takes the record and wraps `within`, e.g. `within_comment(comment) { click_button "Approve" }` with `def within_comment(comment, &) = within("##{dom_id(comment)}", &)`. Put it in a module named after the resource with a `FeatureSpecHelpers` suffix, e.g. `CommentFeatureSpecHelpers`, included only for `type: :feature`, in the same file as the resource's spec helpers module, e.g. `spec/support/comment_spec_helpers.rb`. When a step targets a specific element for the record, e.g. a component, add the element to the name, e.g. `within_post_card(post)` for `Posts::CardComponent`. You MUST NOT write the selector out, e.g. `within("#comment_#{comment.id}")`.
- In feature specs for an API, make requests through `client = ActionDispatch::Integration::Session.new(Rails.application)`, e.g. `client.post api_v1_posts_path` and `client.response`. Start each scenario name with the persona who owns the access token, or with the client when no user owns it, e.g. `scenario "API client writes a post"`.
- In feature specs for an API, authenticate the way the client does. When the API takes an access token, send it in the request headers, e.g. `headers: { "Authorization" => "Bearer <token>" }`. You MUST NOT call `sign_in`.
- In feature specs for an API, check the status and the shape of the body of every response, e.g. `expect(client.response).to have_http_status(:created)` and `expect(client.response.parsed_body).to match("id" => an_instance_of(Integer), "title" => "Hello World")`. Use composable matchers for values the spec cannot know in advance.
- In feature specs for an API, take the data for each request from the response before it, e.g. `client.get api_v1_post_path(client.response.parsed_body["id"])` after creating a post. You MUST NOT look records up in the database or reuse records built with a factory.
- When specs look for the same element on more than one page, write a custom matcher named after what it finds, e.g. `have_welcome_new_author_banner`.
- Always write a custom matcher when one spec checks that an element is there and another checks that it is not, and use the same matcher for both, e.g. `expect(response.body).to have_publish_button_for_post(draft)` and `expect(response.body).not_to have_publish_button_for_post(published_post)`. You MUST NOT check presence and absence with different matchers, e.g. `to have_button("Publish")` and `not_to have_css("form[action='...']")`.
- Give a generic matcher no arguments, e.g. `have_welcome_new_author_banner`. Give a matcher for one record the record as its argument and the suffix `_for_<resource>`, e.g. `have_publish_button_for_post(post)`. Give a matcher for a message the message as a required argument, e.g. `have_flash_notice("Post was updated.")`.
- Define a custom matcher with `matcher`, so it works with both `to` and `not_to` with as little code as it needs, and check the element with a Capybara matcher in its `match` block, e.g. `match { |actual| expect(actual).to have_css("form[action='#{post_publication_path(post)}'] button", text: "Publish") }` in `have_publish_button_for_post`. When the matcher checks one thing, write only `match`, without `notify_expectation_failures`, because RSpec runs `match` for `not_to` too and the option would make it fail when the element is missing. You MUST NOT write a separate matcher for the absence of an element, e.g. `have_no_welcome_new_author_banner`.
- When a matcher only narrows one Capybara matcher, e.g. adds a filter, write it as a method that returns that Capybara matcher and passes its arguments through, e.g. `def have_comment_select(locator = nil, **options) = have_select(locator, class: "comment_select", **options)`. Use `matcher` when it checks more than one thing or builds its own selector.
- Build a complex matcher from simpler ones, combined with `and`. Define each part as a private method inside the matcher, with a `have_` prefix and named after what the part is, e.g. `def have_welcome_heading = have_css("h2", text: "Welcome, new author")` and `def have_first_post_link = have_link("Write your first post", href: new_post_path)`, then `expect(actual).to have_welcome_heading.and have_first_post_link` in `match`. You MUST NOT name a part after a Capybara matcher, e.g. `have_link` or `have_title`, because it would call itself. Only then add a `match_when_negated` block with one `expect(actual).not_to` for each part, e.g. `expect(actual).not_to have_welcome_heading` and `expect(actual).not_to have_first_post_link`, and pass `notify_expectation_failures: true` to both blocks.
- When only one spec file uses a matcher, define it with `matcher` at the bottom of that file, inside the top-level `describe` block, after the examples.
- When more than one spec file uses a matcher, move it to a module in `spec/support`, extended with `RSpec::Matchers::DSL` when it uses `matcher`, and included for every spec type that checks the element, e.g. `type: :request` and `type: :feature`. Keep all the includes for a module in one `RSpec.configure` block in the module's own file, and add a gem's spec type to that block when its specs need the module, e.g. `type: :component`.
- Keep the shared spec code for a resource, including its matchers, in one module named after the resource with a `SpecHelpers` suffix, e.g. `PostSpecHelpers` in `spec/support/post_spec_helpers.rb`. You MUST NOT name it `PostHelpers` or `PostsHelper`. Name a module for generic matchers after what they cover, e.g. `OnboardingSpecHelpers` for `have_welcome_new_author_banner`.
- Give each helper that builds a simple view element a matcher named after the helper with a `have_` prefix, e.g. `have_unknown_value_tag` for `unknown_value_tag`. Put it in a module named after the helper module with a `SpecHelpers` suffix, e.g. `UnknownValuesSpecHelpers` in `spec/support/unknown_values_spec_helpers.rb` for `UnknownValuesHelper`, included for `type: :helper`, `type: :request` and `type: :feature`.
- Check a helper's output in its helper spec with its matcher, e.g. `expect(helper.unknown_value_tag).to have_unknown_value_tag`, and use the matcher in request and feature specs instead of checking the markup, e.g. `expect(response.body).to have_unknown_value_tag`.
- Include setup for form specs with `type: :form`, not with `file_path:`. You MUST NOT tag a form spec with `type: :form` by hand. Do the same for any other spec folder rspec-rails doesn't know, e.g. `spec/actions/` with `:action` and `spec/components/` with `:component`.
- Build the records an example needs inside the example, and name the example after the path it takes, e.g. `post = instance_double(Post, published_at: nil)` in `it "returns the unknown value tag for a draft"`.
- Only write a `context` when several examples share setup that the other examples in the `describe` don't. A `context` MAY hold every example in its `describe` when its name gives the state they run in, e.g. `context "with a published post"`. You MUST NOT write a `context` for one example, and you MUST NOT set up a default with `let` for a `context` to override, other than `current_time`.
- In request specs, the required contexts are the exception to these context rules: write each persona context, each authentication context, e.g. `context "without an access token"`, and `context "with a Turbo Stream"` even when it holds one example. Define the user and the records each persona needs in its own context.
- Only declare a `let` for the setup a `context` is about, so every example in it runs with that setup, even one that doesn't read it: the persona's signed-in `user` and the records that give it its role, e.g. in `context "as a user", "with a post as the author"`; the state the context is named for, e.g. `let(:draft) { create(:post, published_at: nil) }` in `context "with a draft post"`; or setup the examples share, e.g. the comment that each example in `context "with a comment awaiting approval"` approves or rejects.
- You MUST NOT declare a `let` for a record only some examples need, e.g. `let(:other_post)` for the one example that checks another author's draft isn't listed. Build it inside that example, e.g. `create(:post, title: "Their draft", published_at: nil)`.
- Declare a `let` in the `context` it is for. You MUST NOT declare a `let` in a `describe` block, e.g. `let(:published_post)` in `describe "POST /posts/:post_id/comments"`. The only exceptions are `let(:current_time)` at the top of the spec, a stubbed service double in an action spec and the stand-in `record` in a validator spec, following their own instructions. This rule doesn't cover `subject`, e.g. `subject(:post)` in model specs.
- You SHOULD use `let!` for a record that an example checks with `expect { }.to change` or `not_to change`, e.g. `let!(:draft) { create(:post, author: user) }` for `expect { delete post_path(draft) }.to change(Post, :count).by(-1)`. A lazy `let` first read inside the block creates its record there, so the change could come from the factory, not the code under test.
- Also use `let!` when a context's examples need a record to exist without naming it, e.g. `let!(:published_post) { create(:post, title: "Hello World", published_at: Time.zone.now) }` in `context "with a published post"` for `GET /posts`. Otherwise use `let`. When only one example needs the record, call `create` in that example, before the `expect` block.
- In unit specs, e.g. decorator and action specs, build a record with an `instance_double` that stubs only the values the code reads, e.g. `post = instance_double(Post, published_at: nil)`. You MUST NOT use a plain `double`, e.g. `double("post")`.
- When an `instance_double` can't stand in for the record, e.g. the code passes it to a route helper or a form, build it with `build_stubbed`, e.g. `post = build_stubbed(:post, title: "Hello")`.
- Use `create` only when the code needs the record in the database, e.g. when it runs a query, or a request or feature spec loads the record by its ID.
- You SHOULD NOT stub a chain of calls with `receive_message_chain`. Move the chain into a method on the class it starts from, so the spec stubs one method, e.g. a scoped association such as `allow(post).to receive(:approved_comments)` for `post.comments.approved`, or a `perform_later_` method on a job such as `PublishScheduledPostJob.perform_later_for(post)`.
- You SHOULD give each attribute in a factory a random value from Faker, e.g. `name { Faker::Name.name }`, not a fixed one, e.g. `name { "Jane Tester" }`. When a column has to be unique, you SHOULD add a number from a transient `counter` sequence, and build every unique value on the factory from the same counter, not a sequence for each attribute, e.g. `transient { sequence(:counter) }` then `email { Faker::Internet.email(name: "user#{counter}") }`. When a unique value has a set format, build it from the counter with `format`, padded to the format's length, e.g. `issn { format("0000-%04d", counter) }`. You MAY use Faker's `unique` instead, e.g. `Faker::Internet.unique.email`.
- Give a factory a trait for each state a page shows differently, named after the state the app uses, e.g. `:published` or `:archived`. When a job or an action adds values to the record, name the trait after what happened, e.g. `:sent_to_subscribers`. Set the values the state needs, so the record is valid and representative, e.g. `status { :rejected }` and `rejection_reason { Faker::Lorem.sentence }` in `:rejected`.
- Set every value an example checks in the spec, in the example or its context's `let`, e.g. `author = build_stubbed(:user, name: "Jane Tester")` and `post = build_stubbed(:post, author:)` before `expect(post.decorate.author_name).to eq("Jane Tester")`, or `newsletter_id = "newsletter-1"` and `stub_newsletter_create(id: newsletter_id)` before `expect(response).to have_attributes(id: newsletter_id)`. You MUST NOT check against a default from a factory or a stub helper, including the records a factory builds for you, e.g. the author's name from `build_stubbed(:post)`. Leave the values the example doesn't check to the defaults.
- You SHOULD give factories and stub helpers a default for every value they need, so they work with no arguments, e.g. `create(:post)` and `def stub_newsletter_create(id: "newsletter-1")`. Require an argument only when the helper can't pick a default, e.g. `stub_newsletter_client_for(integration)`. Pass a value the spec checks even when it's the same as the default, e.g. `stub_newsletter_create(id: "newsletter-1")`.
- Check against the value you set, e.g. `eq("Jane Tester")`. You SHOULD NOT check against a value read back from a record, e.g. `eq(post.author.name)`. Read from the record when the spec can't set the value, e.g. a record's `id` in `"posts/#{post.id}.json"`, or when a request or feature spec checks a value the example didn't set. When you read back, read the attribute the value is saved in, e.g. `post.summary`. You MUST NOT read it through a method that picks or builds the value, e.g. `post.excerpt`, which returns another attribute when there is no summary, or a decorator method, e.g. `post.decorate.published_on`, because the check then passes whatever the value is. Cover the method's paths in its own model or decorator spec.
- In request and feature specs, you MAY check a value the example didn't set, e.g. a parent's name or a value a trait sets, by reading it from the record through a format helper, e.g. `have_link(format_text(comment.post.magazine.name))` or `format_date(published_post.published_at)`. Set the values the example is about in the spec. You MUST NOT read a value from a record in a check without a format helper, e.g. `have_link(comment.post.magazine.name)`, because Capybara ignores a `nil` locator or `text:`.
- In a JSON body check in a request spec, you MAY read a value the example didn't set from the record's attribute without a format helper, e.g. `"magazine" => { "name" => published_post.magazine.name }`.
- Write each format helper in `spec/support/format_spec_helpers.rb` the same way the app formats the value, and raise when there's no value, e.g. `I18n.l(value, format: :long)` in `format_datetime`. You MUST NOT call the app's own helpers from a format helper, e.g. `date_tag`.
- In request and job specs, when the code under test enqueues jobs, check each job with its arguments, passed with `with`. When it enqueues one job, wrap the call in an `expect` block, e.g. `expect { post post_publication_path(draft) }.to have_enqueued_job(NotifySubscribersJob).with(draft)`. When it enqueues more than one, make the call on its own, then check each job on its own line, e.g. `expect(NotifySubscribersJob).to have_been_enqueued.with(draft)` then `expect(BackupPostJob).to have_been_enqueued.with(draft)`.
- When a spec uses an identifier in more than one place, you SHOULD declare it once, in a local variable in the example, e.g. `newsletter_id = "newsletter-1"`, then use the name everywhere, e.g. `stub_newsletter_create(id: newsletter_id)` and `expect(response.id).to eq(newsletter_id)`. You SHOULD NOT write the same literal twice. When the examples in a context all use it, declare it in a `let` in that context instead, e.g. `let(:newsletter_id) { "newsletter-1" }`. You MUST NOT add a context only to hold the `let`.
- You SHOULD NOT read an identifier out of a fixture in a spec, e.g. `JSON.parse(file_fixture("newsletter_create.json").read)["id"]`. Declare it in the spec and pass it to the stub helper, which puts it into the reply.
- In a `not_to` check, you SHOULD take the value it looks for from the records the spec set up, e.g. `their_draft = create(:post, published_at: nil)` then `expect(response.body).not_to have_link(their_draft.title)`, not a value you wrote in, e.g. `not_to have_link("Their draft")`. A `not_to` check with a value that doesn't match the setup, e.g. a title the factory never gave the post, passes even when the code is wrong.
- When you check that the code leaves a value alone, check it against the record's value from before the code ran with `not_to change`, e.g. `expect { patch post_path(draft), params: { post: { title: "New title" } } }.not_to change { draft.reload.title }`. You MUST NOT check it with `not_to` and a value you wrote in, e.g. `expect(draft.reload.title).not_to eq("New title")`, because it passes when the code changes the value to anything else. RSpec doesn't support `to` after `not_to change`.
- When the code generates a string with a known format, match it with `match`, or `a_string_matching` inside another matcher, and a regexp for the whole string, with what the spec knows written in, e.g. `expect(result.token).to match(/\A[\w-]{22}\z/)` for a token made with `SecureRandom.urlsafe_base64` in `SharePostForm#submit`, or `have_requested_newsletter_create(headers: { "X-Request-Id" => a_string_matching(/\A\h{8}-\h{4}-\h{4}-\h{4}-\h{12}\z/) })` for a request ID sent in a header. Use `a_kind_of(String)` only as a last resort, when the string has no format the spec can describe.
- When the code saves something made from a generated value, check that too, e.g. `expect(post.reload.preview_token_digest).to eq(Digest::SHA256.hexdigest(result.token))`.
